messages.content:
You are an independent classifier in a blinded experiment about a book of
biblical symbolism. The consensus responses below were produced without access
to the book. Compare them with the book's entry.

TERM
Sign

BLIND CONSENSUS RESPONSES
RESPONSE A
{
  "primary_meaning": "In mainstream Christian teaching, a 'sign' (Hebrew 'oth, Greek semeion) is understood as a visible act, event, or object that points beyond itself to God's presence, power, and purpose — most characteristically a miraculous work that authenticates God's messenger and reveals divine identity. The paradigmatic usage is in John's Gospel, where Jesus' miracles are called 'signs' precisely because their significance lies not in the wonder itself but in what they disclose about who Jesus is (his glory, messiahship, and divine sonship), calling observers to faith.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "John 2:11 (the first sign at Cana manifesting Jesus' glory)",
    "John 20:30-31 (signs written 'that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ')",
    "Exodus 4:1-9 and Exodus 7:3 (signs authenticating Moses before Israel and Pharaoh)",
    "Deuteronomy 4:34; 6:22 ('signs and wonders' of the Exodus as God's self-revelation)",
    "Isaiah 7:14 (the sign of Immanuel given to Ahaz)",
    "Acts 2:22 (Jesus 'attested by God with mighty works and wonders and signs')",
    "John 3:2 (Nicodemus: 'no one can do these signs unless God is with him')",
    "Hebrews 2:3-4 (God bearing witness by signs and wonders)"
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "Covenant sign or seal: a physical marker God attaches to a covenant as a perpetual reminder and pledge — the rainbow, circumcision, and the Sabbath. In Reformed and Catholic theology this extends to the sacraments (baptism, Lord's Supper) as visible signs and seals of invisible grace, following Augustine's definition of a sacrament as a visible sign of an invisible reality (cf. Romans 4:11, circumcision as 'sign and seal').",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 9:12-17 (rainbow as sign of the covenant)",
        "Genesis 17:11 (circumcision as sign of the covenant)",
        "Exodus 31:13-17 (Sabbath as a sign between God and Israel)",
        "Romans 4:11 (circumcision as a sign and seal of righteousness by faith)",
        "Ezekiel 20:12,20 (Sabbath as sign)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Eschatological or apocalyptic indicator: 'signs of the times' and cosmic signs preceding the end — celestial disturbances, wars, false christs, and the 'sign of the Son of Man' — read as markers of Christ's return and the close of the age. This usage dominates prophecy-focused and dispensational teaching.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 24:3,30 ('what will be the sign of your coming?'; 'the sign of the Son of Man')",
        "Luke 21:11,25 (signs in sun, moon, and stars)",
        "Matthew 16:3 (interpreting the signs of the times)",
        "Joel 2:30-31 / Acts 2:19 (wonders in heaven, signs on earth)",
        "Revelation 12:1,3; 15:1 (great signs in heaven)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Sign as warning, judgment, or occasion of unbelief: demands for signs are portrayed negatively as faithless testing of God; the only sign given a wicked generation is the 'sign of Jonah' (Christ's death and resurrection, and implicitly a call to repentance under threat of judgment). Also false signs performed by deceivers.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 12:38-40; 16:1-4 (an evil generation seeks a sign; the sign of Jonah)",
        "1 Corinthians 1:22 ('Jews demand signs')",
        "John 4:48 ('unless you see signs and wonders you will not believe')",
        "2 Thessalonians 2:9 and Matthew 24:24 (false signs and wonders of deceivers)",
        "Mark 8:11-12 (no sign given to this generation)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Prophetic sign-act: symbolic actions performed by prophets (and by prophets' own lives or children) as enacted messages of coming judgment or salvation — e.g., Isaiah walking naked, Ezekiel's dramatizations, Hosea's marriage; the prophet himself as a sign to the people.",
      "basis": [
        "Isaiah 8:18 ('I and the children the LORD has given me are signs')",
        "Isaiah 20:3 (Isaiah's nakedness as a sign against Egypt)",
        "Ezekiel 4:1-3; 12:6,11; 24:24,27 ('Ezekiel shall be a sign to you')",
        "Hosea 1:2-9 (Hosea's marriage and children as enacted signs)"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Confirmatory sign granted to individuals as assurance of God's word or calling (e.g., Gideon's fleece, the sign to Ahaz, the shepherds' sign of the manger) — a personal token verifying a specific promise rather than a public miracle.",
      "basis": [
        "Judges 6:36-40 (Gideon's fleece)",
        "Exodus 3:12 (the sign given to Moses)",
        "1 Samuel 10:1-9 (signs confirming Saul's anointing)",
        "Luke 2:12 ('this will be a sign to you: a baby wrapped in swaddling cloths')",
        "2 Kings 20:8-11 (the sign of the shadow for Hezekiah)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "Charismatic/Pentecostal reading emphasizing signs (with tongues, healing, and wonders) as ongoing marks accompanying believers and the gospel's advance in every era, per the longer ending of Mark; contested by cessationists who limit authenticating signs to the apostolic period.",
      "basis": [
        "Mark 16:17-20 ('these signs will accompany those who believe')",
        "Acts 2:43; 5:12; 14:3 (signs and wonders through the apostles)",
        "2 Corinthians 12:12 ('the signs of a true apostle')",
        "Romans 15:19 (gospel confirmed by the power of signs and wonders)"
      ],
      "prominence": "minority"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "'Sign' is one of the more stable terms in biblical interpretation: virtually all traditions (Catholic, Orthodox, Protestant, and academic biblical scholarship) agree on the core sense of a pointer to divine reality rather than an end in itself, with Johannine usage treated as the theological center. Disagreements are contextual rather than definitional — which category of sign is in view (authenticating miracle, covenant marker, eschatological portent, sacrament, prophetic act) and whether sign-working continues today (continuationist vs. cessationist). The scholarly literature also notes the deliberate Johannine contrast between 'signs' (semeia) and mere 'wonders' (terata): signs demand interpretation and faith, not just amazement. Because the term is genuinely polyvalent across Scripture, an author could plausibly foreground any of the listed senses, but the 'pointer to God's identity and action, especially Jesus' authenticated identity' reading is the recognizable default in commentaries, Bible dictionaries (e.g., entries on semeion), and catechetical teaching."
}

RESPONSE B
{
  "primary_meaning": "A “sign” is most commonly understood functionally as a visible event, act, object, or miracle that points beyond itself to divine activity and confirms God’s message, promise, presence, or the authority of God’s messenger. It does not have one fixed symbolic referent across Scripture.",
  "primary_basis": [
    "Exodus 4:1–9, 29–31 — miraculous signs authenticate Moses’ divine commission.",
    "Exodus 7:3; Deuteronomy 4:34 — signs and wonders reveal God’s power in the exodus.",
    "Isaiah 7:14 — a divinely given sign confirms a prophetic promise.",
    "John 2:11 — Jesus’ sign reveals his glory and leads disciples to believe.",
    "John 20:30–31 — Jesus’ signs are recorded to support faith in his identity.",
    "Acts 2:22; Hebrews 2:3–4 — signs authenticate Jesus and the apostolic proclamation.",
    "Romans 4:11 — circumcision is called a sign and seal of covenantal righteousness."
  ],
  "alternatives": [
    {
      "meaning": "A miraculous work or “wonder,” emphasizing supernatural power rather than a symbolic object or encoded meaning.",
      "basis": [
        "Exodus 7:3",
        "Acts 2:22",
        "Acts 4:30",
        "2 Corinthians 12:12"
      ],
      "prominence": "dominant"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A covenant marker that identifies a people, recalls a promise, or signifies an enduring relationship with God.",
      "basis": [
        "Genesis 9:12–17 — the rainbow as covenant sign.",
        "Genesis 17:11 — circumcision as covenant sign.",
        "Exodus 31:13, 16–17 — the Sabbath as a sign between God and Israel.",
        "Romans 4:11 — circumcision as sign and seal."
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A prophetic symbol or omen, including an enacted sign, that depicts or anticipates a coming judgment, deliverance, or historical event.",
      "basis": [
        "Isaiah 8:18",
        "Isaiah 20:3",
        "Ezekiel 4:1–3",
        "Ezekiel 12:6, 11"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "An eschatological indicator marking the approach of divine judgment, Christ’s return, or the consummation of history.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 24:3, 24, 30",
        "Luke 21:7, 11, 25",
        "Revelation 12:1, 3",
        "Revelation 15:1"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "In sacramental theology, a material element or rite that signifies—and in many traditions also conveys or participates in—divine grace.",
      "basis": [
        "Romans 4:11",
        "Matthew 26:26–28",
        "1 Corinthians 10:16",
        "1 Peter 3:21"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A specific reference to Jesus’ death, burial, and resurrection through the “sign of Jonah,” rather than a general meaning of the word sign.",
      "basis": [
        "Matthew 12:38–40",
        "Matthew 16:1–4",
        "Luke 11:29–30"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    },
    {
      "meaning": "A deceptive or counterfeit supernatural manifestation that supports false teaching or rebellion; a sign therefore does not automatically prove divine approval.",
      "basis": [
        "Deuteronomy 13:1–3",
        "Matthew 24:24",
        "2 Thessalonians 2:9–10",
        "Revelation 13:13–14"
      ],
      "prominence": "common"
    }
  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": false,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "There is broad consensus about the term’s general function—something perceptible that points beyond itself or authenticates a claim—but no settled, single symbolic meaning. Its referent depends on context: miracle, covenant marker, prophetic token, eschatological omen, sacramental element, or deceptive wonder."
}

RESPONSE C
{
  "primary_meaning": "A miraculous deed, wonder, or token performed by God or His authorized messengers that authenticates divine authority, reveals God's glory or presence, and is intended to produce faith or obedience",
  "primary_basis": [

  ],
  "has_settled_consensus": true,
  "confidence": "high",
  "notes": "In both Testaments the core semantic range of 'sign' (Heb. ʾôt; Gk. sēmeion) centers on divine authentication and revelation; the miracle/wonder sense is dominant in Christian proclamation and Johannine theology, while covenantal and eschatological uses remain standard and non-contradictory within the broader category. No major Christian tradition redefines the term outside this family of meanings."
}

BOOK ENTRY
A prophecy given in advance — often a prophet's lived story — whose fulfillment testifies; not a wonder performed on demand.

BOOK'S COMMON-VIEW NOTE, IF PRESENT
Commonly taught: a miraculous act pointing to God's power and Christ's identity.

SCRIPTURE REFERENCES PRINTED WITH THE ENTRY
(Isa 7:14; Ezek 24:24; Luke 11:30) · see Signs and Similitudes, ch. 3

AVAILABLE KJV EXCERPTS
Isaiah 7:14 — Therefore the Lord himself shall give you a sign; Behold, a virgin shall conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
Ezekiel 24:24 — Thus Ezekiel is unto you a sign: according to all that he hath done shall ye do: and when this cometh, ye shall know that I am the Lord GOD.
Luke 11:30 — For as Jonas was a sign unto the Ninevites, so shall also the Son of man be to this generation.

CLASSIFY THE RELATIONSHIP

First reduce both readings to their minimum core identifications. Do not let
extra detail create an artificial disagreement.

- MATCH: the core identifications are equivalent. Differences are merely
  wording or immaterial detail.
- REFINED: the book preserves the consensus's general referent or category but
  materially changes its extension, boundary, conditions, or precision. A
  narrowing may reject some cases the broader consensus admits; a broadening
  may admit cases it excludes. This is real disagreement at the boundary, but
  not replacement of the central referent.
- DIVERGENT: the cores materially contradict. Both claims cannot be true of the
  same referent in the same context and sense; accepting the book requires
  rejecting or replacing the consensus identification. A source and its
  product remain different referents when the book explicitly denies their
  identity, even if they are causally related.
- NOVEL: no recognizable consensus or listed alternative covers the book's
  core identification. Novelty is absence from consensus, not contradiction.

Use `core_relation` to expose the relationship at the center and
`extension_relation` to expose disagreement over the cases covered. A REFINED
verdict must state what cases the book adds, excludes, or reclassifies. A
DIVERGENT verdict must identify a replaced referent or material contradiction,
not merely a narrower boundary.

Treat the two axes independently. A core-divergent reading may still retain
some cases covered by the consensus while rejecting its central identification;
therefore DIVERGENT does not require disjoint extensions. Conversely, a
narrowed extension is REFINED only when the consensus's central referent or
category remains intact.

Also judge whether the citations printed with the glossary entry alone provide
strong, partial, or insufficient support. Do not yet decide whether a divergent
full chapter is persuasive; that is a separate stage.
